utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we give you, Mr. Tieger, the opportunity to call your next witness, I'd like to deliver a decision on the sixth batch of 92 bis witnesses. This is a decision on the sixth batch of 92 bis witnesses. I briefly recall that the Chamber is seized of the Prosecution's motion for the admission of 92 bis evidence filed on the 6th of June, 2003, seventh motion, and of another motion filed on the 29th of May, 2003 in which the Prosecution submitted the report of expert witness Ewa Tabeau under Rule 92 bis. Madam Registrar, may I ask you to -- I take it at least you have received a handout to be - yes - distributed. It's a list showing the names of the 92 bis witnesses who are not required to attend for cross-examination. Could it be distributed to the parties. I will deliver the Chamber's decision concerning these witnesses. With respect to witnesses Zujo and Mesic, the Prosecution agreed to the Defence's suggestion that the Prosecution review and resubmit the material in a more orderly fashion. In respect of witness Dobraca, the Prosecution indicated to the Chamber last Friday, the 24th of June, when it was explicitly invited to give its comment, that the material for this witness is also under review. The Chamber therefore grants the Prosecution's request to defer the Chamber's decision in respect of these three witnesses. Mr. Tieger, the Chamber would like to know when it will receive the material in a more orderly fashion. As far as expert witnesses Hunt, Wright, and Clark are concerned, the Chamber, in accordance with the submissions of both the Defence and the Prosecution, has no objection to the admission into evidence of the requested material and will not ask the witnesses to appear for cross-examination. In respect of witness Kaiser, having read the material proposed for admission, the Chamber has decided to admit the report. The Chamber will not admit either of the transcripts at this time, but invites the Prosecution to inform the Chamber about whether it intended to seek admission of the transcripts in their entirety, since no portions are highlighted. Witness Kaiser will not be required to appear for cross-examination. In relation to witness Tabeau, the report, as shown in the handout, is admitted. Neither the Prosecution nor the Defence requested that the witness appear for cross-examination. However, the Chamber would like to leave open the possibility of asking the witness Tabeau to provide more details about the conclusions reached in her report and will decide at a later stage whether she should be called. I now turn to witness Thompson. Since the witness is not very precise about the sources of the information in his report, the Chamber agrees with the parties that the witness should be called for cross-examination. The material associated with this witness is therefore not shown in the handout. Material relating to this witness will be admitted into evidence, subject to any further objections, at the time the witness is heard in cross-examination. The report of witness Donia describes itself as a background report and develops a thesis on the genesis of Republika Srpska. The subject of the report naturally calls for selection of materials and interpretation of facts. No analysis of a significant historical episode has ever passed unchallenged. The Defence may well decide to challenge Donia's thesis during the presentation of its case, if we come to that. However, the Chamber feels that it is important to take the opportunity to test this report already at this stage of the proceedings. Due to the so-called background nature of the report, the Chamber will not, however, allow the parties to spend a great deal of time on it. At the same time, the Chamber intends to give each party a fair opportunity to challenge the views developed by the other party's background experts, and to test the material which supports those views. In respect of Donia, the Chamber has therefore decided the following: The Chamber will admit his report and allow the Defence approximately three hours to cross-examine him. In addition, in order for cross-examination to be efficient and focused, the Defence may apply for admission of small portions of Donia's testimony in other proceedings. And of course the Chamber would not be surprised if that would very much focus on those portions where Donia is cross-examined. Such an application for admission of small portions should be made not later than one week prior to the date on which Donia is scheduled to testify. The Prosecution will also be allowed to apply for the admission of small portions of Donia's evidence in previous cases. This should be done no later than the day before the witness is scheduled to testify. The Chamber requests that the Prosecution submit the material admitted through this decision to Madam Registrar, and in due course, Madam Registrar will assign exhibit numbers to those items and inform the parties and the Chamber. I also kindly ask Madam Registrar to file the handout. This concludes the Chamber's decision on the sixth batch of 92 bis witnesses. Then, Mr. Tieger, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just raise a couple of very short practical points?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: One is that recently the Trial Chamber, Mr. Zahar specifically, very helpfully responded to requests from me that these handouts, which must exist on a computer, could also be sent by e-mail. It's useful to us to keep them in an electronic file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll ask the legal officer to get in such with Mr. Zahar to take care of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think there may be a tiny backlog on that and it would be much appreciated if we could have a complete batch of these handouts. I see nodding and that's obviously not a problem. The second point is only this: In the light of what Your Honour has said in relation to Mr. Donia, may I simply through Your Honours, and since we're all in Court, particularly ask for close liaison in relation to that witness. A date for him has not been indicated in any draft schedule. He's a floater, in a sense, and given the timetable that Your Honour indicates and given that when one is trying to deal with these advanced matters for witness one is at the same time dealing with another witness, if we could have especially close liaison and as much notice as possible of what is contemplated in relation to him, that would be greatly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can imagine that you did not schedule him, Mr. Tieger, because the OTP objected against cross-examination as being no need to cross-examine Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I understand the reasons and we have a high degree of cooperation over these things, Your Honour, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. You have the commitment of Mr. Tieger. Then your next witness. No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be Mr. Tupajic, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tupajic, I take it. Before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tupajic. Please be seated. Mr. Tupajic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Tieger, counsel for the Prosecution. Examined by Mr. Tieger:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tupajic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to begin by providing the Court with some indication of your basic personal and political background, and I will do that by simply reciting some of those markers as in summary form and just ask for your confirmation if that's accurate. First of all, I understand you were born and raised in Sokolac, where you went to elementary school and high school.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not receive English translation on channel 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born in the village of Knezina, which is a village in the municipality of Sokolac, and this is where I also completed my primary education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1978, you graduated from the faculty of mechanical engineering in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And thereafter worked at the Famos factory in Hrasnica for approximately six years before returning to Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In August of 1990, you joined the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning briefly to your professional background, until 1991 you were in charge of production and later head of the department at a factory in Sokolac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a factory for the production of bearings that was jointly built by Unis and a company from Geteborg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991, you became president of the Sokolac Municipal Assembly when the previous president left.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And in the meantime, sometime in May or June, the factory had stopped working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April 1992, you became president of the Sokolac Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1996, you were elected to the National Assembly as an SDS candidate?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from 1998 until last year, you served as president of the SDS deputies' club.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so the Court is aware of that, the cessation of your term in the Assembly and as president of the deputies' club was at the behest of the special representative?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the decision of the high representative on the removal of the representatives from Republika Srpska, amongst whom I also found myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also became a member of the SDS Main Board in 2002?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was in 2002, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that was an example of mistranslation or misstatement on my part, but yes, I understood that that was in 2002. Thank you. Can you tell us quickly the approximate population of Sokolac municipality in 1990 and 1991 and the breakdown of Serbs and Muslims, of their population within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: According to the 1991 census, which was the last census in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the municipality of Sokolac had 15.000 inhabitants of whom 70 per cent were Serbs, 30 per cent were Muslims, and there were only a couple of dozen Croats who resided in the territory of Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, earlier you indicated that you became president of the Sokolac Crisis Staff in April of 1992. Is that when the Sokolac Crisis Staff was established?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. As far as I can remember, the first session was held on the 6th of April pursuant to a telegram and an order that arrived from Mr. Karadzic and which was sent not only to us in Sokolac, but I suppose at the time, which later turned to be true, was sent to other municipalities as well. Those were either new Serbian municipalities or the municipalities that had existed before, that were established after the elections. So this telegram and this order was sent to all the municipalities in the then Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I ask that an exhibit be placed before the witness, and that exhibit is one familiar to the Court, it's the instructions of 19 December 1991. I recall the Court's previous admonition, Your Honour, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We also do know that there are many versions, some of them in evidence. This is the handwritten number 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. And we'll again do our best to ensure it's not duplicated again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not clear. It's the handwritten and circled 27 copy which bears the copy number 93, 093.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, looking at this document, copy number 93 of the instructions for the organisation and activities of the organs of the Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in a state of emergency, are you familiar with that document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the document, although I never had it on my files. It was sent by the Main Board to the presidents of the municipal boards. It was confidential. I believe that we discussed this document at the sessions of the Municipal Board, but we members of the Municipal Board were never familiarised with the integral text of the instruction. However, we were familiar with the contents, the essence of the instruction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, looking at portions of the document, can you tell us whether or not some of the steps enumerated in the document under the first level were implemented in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this part of the document deals with the necessity to provide security, even physical security to certain facilities in municipalities, and in view of the fact that the most important facility for us or, rather, the most important feature was the source of Biostica River, because it is the source of potable water for the entire municipality, we got from the TO staff resources to lay minefields around this source because it is close to Knezina village, securing it in this way, because we were afraid that some extremist group could carry out the sabotage action of poisoning the water. Then we needed to build up stocks of the basic necessities in Sokolac, expecting certain developments in the future.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with reference to the security measures taken in connection with the water supply, is that a reference to step 6 under the first level of Variant A? "The organisation and protection for important facilities Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in the municipality is to be strengthened."

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were other steps enumerated in the document also implemented?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I think the Territorial Defence Staff carried out certain preparations within its own purview, such as checking and analysing the condition and the readiness of all the weapons stockpiled in the TO depot. That was normal for peacetime. And they also checked the condition and readiness of communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned at the very end of your discussion about the steps taken in connection with the water supply the need to build up stocks of basic necessities. Can you tell us any specific actions -- can you tell us first whether that was a reference to step 7 in the document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us any specific actions undertaken pursuant to step 7?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I remember that these activities were handled by the President of the Executive Board at the time, but there was one occasion when we went together to Sarajevo to visit the Klas enterprise which, among other things, had certain warehouses holding wheat crops. Drago Podinic was in that enterprise. And there were also wheat warehouses in the surrounding area of Pale. And we had certain talks with these people but without particular success, because this Drago Podinic, the director, had his own relationships, better relationships, with certain agricultural cooperatives, and he was not particularly interested in providing us with what we needed. And we had asked him to look into the matter because we did not know exactly what quantities were in the warehouses, and most of the wheat came from Serbia. So our request to him was to ensure that they are filled, these warehouses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Step 3 of the document provides for the establishment or formation of a Crisis Staff of the Serb people in the municipality. Do you know why that step was not taken until the receipt of the telegram from Dr. Karadzic in early April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: We officially established the Crisis Staff of Sokolac municipality after receiving the telegram from Mr. Karadzic. To this day, I don't understand completely whether these were supposed to be staffs on the level of SDS or on the level of municipalities involving presidents of other parties, because in certain municipalities there were SDS crisis staffs, whereas in Sokolac, since we had complete control over the municipalities, there were no particular activities to set up an SDS Crisis Staff, and if one was formed at all, it was formed as part of the Municipal Board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, can I next turn your attention to an excerpt from your daily agenda or notebook that appears closest to an entry of 17 January 1992. And actually, looking more carefully at the preceding page and the page on which the particular entry to which I want to direct your attention appears, it seems there's a reference to January 17, 1991, and January 22, 1991. Can you tell us first, looking at your diary or journal or agenda, whether that's actually a reference -- that's a reference correctly to 1991 or it's actually a reference to 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I wrote 1991 by mistake. It was in fact 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I failed to ask for exhibit numbers --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It will be Exhibit P827.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Next time if you use page numbering, Mr. Tieger, it would be a good idea not to give the same number to every page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That would seem to defeat the purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tupajic, I'd like to direct your attention to a list of names that appears, I believe, at the ERN 0115-1332, and in particular to the line "Rajko Dukic and Crisis Staff, 277-001." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us first who Rajko Dukic was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Rajko Dukic was born in Milici municipality. As far as I know, he was then member of the Main Board, and for a short while he was also President of the Executive Board of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell the Court what this excerpt is a reference to? What Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I think -- I think this is a reference to the Crisis Staff on the level of the Serbian Democratic Party of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it was known even then. And this is a telephone number where he could be reached. Somebody else wrote the number in their own hand in my agenda, because at the time I didn't know Mr. Dukic at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn our attention next briefly to the -- some of the functions and activities of the Crisis Staff in Sokolac, and may I ask that the next exhibit be placed before the witness. That bears the ERN of 0115-1663. And, Your Honour, may that be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P828.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, P828 is a decision of the Sokolac Crisis Staff that bears the date May 29, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It indicates in item 1 that the following members of the Sokolac Crisis Staff bear the status of mobilised persons. Can you explain that briefly to the Court, the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, in the department of the Defence Ministry that existed in Sokolac municipality, as in every other municipality, all able-bodied men fit for military service had to be registered and had to have a certain assignment. Most of them were assigned to the units of the army of Republika Srpska, a certain number was assigned to the Ministry of the Interior, a certain number had labour assignments, and only we in the Crisis Staff had a sort of labour assignment but without it being officially assigned. We received information from Mr. Ceranic, head of the Crisis Staff, that in view of the work we were doing, we will have the benefit of service time spent in this job being counted double, as other mobilised people have. I asked on that occasion that we receive more detailed information on what we were supposed to do from the body that set up the Crisis Staff in the first place. Of course this time of service was never counted double in our total years of service, although we did spend some time on the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Item 2 of the decision reflected in P828 states that "The above mentioned members of the Crisis Staff are obliged to ensure the functioning of authority, commercial and social life at the level of the Municipality, collaborating with the responsible commands of the Serbian Army and with the Government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on all vital issues."

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that accurately reflect the role of the Crisis Staff or are there aspects of the Crisis Staff's function that you'd like to elaborate on in connection with its obligations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Essentially, yes, it does capture the role of the Crisis Staff, although here, in addition to communicating with the responsible commands of the army, we also communicated with police stations that had an important role in providing governance in Sokolac municipality, and there were a number of other vital issues to be handled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we can look at a few of the records of the Sokolac Crisis Staff in that connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May the next exhibit be placed before the witness. That's 0115-1514 through 1515, the conclusions of the Sokolac Crisis Staff from 20 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be, may I suggest, P829.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, let me direct your attention to conclusion number 4 of P829, which states that "Competent organs should carry out the order issued by Ministry of Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina within a given period, provided that, prior to that, the President of the Crisis Staff and commander of TO staff meet with the minister of defence on account of the issue of keeping a part of the equipment in the territory of the Sokolac Municipality." Could you tell us what order of the Ministry of Defence was the subject of this conclusion and anything else about that conclusion which needs to be elaborated.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: In the days preceding this, there was a major operation wherein a considerable amount of weapons and equipment were evacuated from the depot in Faletici near Sarajevo, and that depot then belonged to the republican staff of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was holding stockpiles of weapons and equipment for the reserve force, of course before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. A considerable part of that equipment was exported, taken away to various places including Sokolac, including also Pale and Mokro, and the order of the Ministry of Defence was to concentrate all that equipment in one place. However, our people in the TO staff, since they played a certain part in the transport and stocking of weapons and equipment, tried to keep a certain quantity together with accompanying documentation. For instance, they thought they did not have enough communication devices, and in their estimate they needed more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I comment something? It's a little bit -- maybe it's simply a coincidence, but we were supplied on the 18th of May with a list of potential exhibits, and then we were supplied more recently with another list of potential exhibits which mainly related to diary entries. The list on the 18th of May was quite long. It contained 65 or 66 files, something like that. It may be just coincidence, but neither of Exhibits 828 nor 829 is on that list. So in the very early batch of exhibits we get we find, extraordinarily enough, that those items were not in that rather large quantity of material. It's a -- it's a bit of a coincidence. It may be just that, and maybe I'm missing something, but we have a lot of items dated the 20th of May on that list, but not this one. And then the previous one, I think, was 20th of April, and the previous one was 29th of May. If I'm assured that this is just a coincidence with these first two items and that this is not gong to be a repeated pattern then I'll feel more comfortable, but if we're going to get a whole batch of exhibits which, extraordinarily enough, don't coincide with the rather large quantity of materials supplied to us, then I am going to be more concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I'm sorry if that's the case. I think Mr. Stewart knows I've always made myself available to the extent humanly possible to advise him as soon as I knew of the even particular exhibits I intended to use in my presentation. As far as I know, yes, it is just a coincidence. It's certainly not by any means an effort to keep from the Defence any understanding of the items we intend to present, and I'm more than happy at any time, including the first break or even now, to advise Mr. Stewart of the items I intend to use in the course of this particular presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm considerably reassured. It's perfectly true, I acknowledge that whole-heartedly, it's perfectly true that Mr. Tieger and I in relation to a number of witnesses have had very cooperative communication, so there's no question of that, and it appears this may be just coincidence. I wanted to raise it now. If it is, then as I said, I'm perfectly happy. So it seems that we can sort this out without too much difficulty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Your Honour, I'd like the witness to be presented with -- I'd like to have two documents marked because they're very closely related. The first is ET 0124-6838. The second is ET 0124-6884.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar. The first one would be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the second one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm happy to say, Your Honour, that was on that original list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If it's helpful, I don't know exactly when this was provided to Mr. Stewart, but he does have the most current list, which is the three-page document which has 28 enumerated items.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, unless I have the order confused, P830 is a document dated May 11, 1992, reflecting a document sent by the government secretary Nedeljko Lakic, asking for six tons of food to be provided to the Crisis Staff of Vogosca from Sokolac, and P831 is a document from the 9th of May, 1992, asking Sokolac to provide five tons of food for the needs of the Crisis Staff of Ilijas. In both cases the issued goods are to be billed to the budget of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you know how the government determined both the need on the part of Vogosca and Ilijas for food, on the one hand, and the ability of Sokolac to provide such food?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I suppose that this request to the Sokolac municipality by the government came after requests from Vogosca and Ilijas, which had it much harder. At that time, we were conducting certain activities precisely with a view to providing reserves of some basic necessities in cooperation with certain enterprises such as Romaninka and Romanija Sokolac, who imported food mainly in barter deals with Serbia, and the level of reserves in Sokolac at the time was relatively good. At certain -- at that time, we even had surpluses of certain foods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the government determined that Vogosca and Ilijas needed food, that Sokolac had food, and arranged for the transfer of that food to the -- to those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: No. They asked from us to deliver certain quantities of food, and I suppose that our companies, using their own vehicles, supplied those foods. I believe that it had been coordinated in terms of the types of food, but this request of the government was complied with by the Crisis Staff, and this message was passed on to either one or both of these companies. I don't know which one. And they were the ones that implemented the request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'd like to look quickly at another exhibit. That's ET 0115-1554.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, P832 is a document that reflects conclusions of the Crisis Staff of Sokolac municipality from May 5, 1992. The first conclusion addresses the issue of the Sokolac psychiatric hospital, and reflects in the last sentence that: "The Crisis Staff shall forward the mentioned report to the Prime Minister and the Ministry of Health of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Is this a reflection of further coordination with and contact with the republic level authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: The psychiatric hospital of Sokolac, at the beginning of the war, was nothing but a burden to us, to the Crisis Staff. It was the biggest psychiatric hospital in Bosnia-Herzegovina before the war, and it still is. It has a number, a great number of patients. When the war started, nobody looked after those patients. At the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. initiative of the chief administrator of the hospital, we discussed the problems that the staff and the patients of the hospital faced, and we wanted to deal with the problem. It was the Ministry of Health and the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were supposed to deal with the problem, but we ourselves took it upon ourselves to collect information and to forward this information to the competent ministry and the government that would then try and solve at least part of the hospital's problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we -- I'd like to direct our attention next to decisions and orders to -- or within Sokolac municipality from the Crisis Staff to local organs. And if I could turn your attention first to the next exhibit, which is 0115-1513.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move to that, could I ask one additional question. Mr. Tupajic, the document we just discussed on the psychiatric hospitals, what was the use of receiving reports including the ethnicity of the patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the psychiatric hospital of Sokolac, this problem has still not been resolved. A great number of patients, I don't know how many, come from the area of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was the case then and it is still the case. And this was done in order to try and show the competent organs of the republic that help was needed. This is how the hospital always functioned. All the municipalities and the competent ministries were obliged to co-finance the work of this hospital. The debts from the war still persist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... stop you. In these conclusions, the information should include the municipalities where they come from, that's what seems to be the core of your answer, but it also mentions the ethnicity. It reads: "Information on the number of patients, their ethnicity, and municipalities that they come from." Your answer seems to focus on the last one, whereas my question was about ethnicity. What difference does it make whether a patient is -- a psychiatric patient is Serb, Croat, Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a matter of fact, you can see from the second part of the conclusion, Mr. President, this was not important to us. However, we believed that this is information that would be requested from us from the ministry as in the meantime there had been some sort of restructuring. We wanted to provide the government with comprehensive information based on which it would see what realistic measures it could take. In the second part of the conclusion, we ask from the management of the hospital to show a completely identical attitude towards all the patients in the hospital and to behave towards all the same -- all of them in the same way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In what way realistic measures to be taken could be different on the basis of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment, we did not expect it to be realistically possible from the Ministry of Health of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to receive anything from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is, we did not expect the Republika Srpska to get anything from Bosnia and Herzegovina. But we wanted to get the competent ministry on board, because by law it should have been responsible for the functioning and work of the psychiatric hospital. It was a state hospital, it was not a local health institution such as, for example, a medical centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. None of your answers addressed the matter I raised. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't note whether 0115-1511 had yet received an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, P833 is an order of the Sokolac municipality Crisis Staff of 20 April, 1992, that the officials of Sokolac public security station together with JNA security organs should work on identifying those involved in the theft of the military equipment from Faletici. And in items 2 and 3 -- that is reflected in -- you don't have that in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. I have a different order before me. No. Again I have two of the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just see. 833 is the 20 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the relevant ERN is 0115-1511. The date of this order is 20 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not the one that has been distributed to us as being 833.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry for that confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Distributed was last four digits 1513, dated 21st of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we undo this, let me just proceed to that particular item as P833.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, Mr. Tieger, I'd like to draw your attention to the fact if we spend the time as we did on one of these exhibits, it would take us 45 minutes for just distribution of these kind of exhibits, so if the logistics could be better organised then that would certainly save us half an hour a day. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, do you still have that same document that you were just looking at in front of you, the document dated 21 April of 1992? It was --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I have. But I still don't have the document that you have just mentioned, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll just look at this document. P833 is an order of the Sokolac municipality Crisis Staff dated 21 April 1992, and it reflects an order that the municipal Secretariat for National Defence of the Sokolac municipality is obliged to immediately take all legal measures against persons who did not respond to the call for mobilisation. In item II it directs that the municipal Secretariat for National Defence will cooperate with the military police in taking legal measures against persons who deserted, and in item III it indicates that the order comes into effect immediately. So does this order, sir, reflect the Crisis Staff's directions to the municipal secretariat to take appropriate actions or actions it deemed appropriate in connection with this issue?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether such actions were taken?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: They were taken. I don't know how efficient they were. I believe that there was never 100 per cent efficiency in their implementation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And can we look next at the document to which I was previously referring, the 20 April 1992 order, ERN ET 0115-1511.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, in relation to the previous document, we now know that were not -- the measures taken were not full hundred per cent efficient but what they were is still totally unclear apart from that there were legal measures and apart from all legal measures. Will we find some information about the type of action taken?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, before we address this current document, the Court noted that although you indicated that the measures taken were not 100 per cent efficient, I failed to ask you to indicate to the best of your recollection what measures were taken by the municipal Secretariat for National Defence in response to the order of the Crisis Staff on 21 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: What was to be done by the Secretariat of the National Defence in keeping with the law was to file reports against the people who did not respond. In the second part of this order, it says that the military police, which existed as part of the 1st Romanija Brigade of the JNA, could bring in people that failed to comply with their legal obligations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us whether those steps were indeed taken, that is whether reports were filed and people were brought in in response to item II for failing to report or for deserting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I believe so, Mr. Prosecutor. I don't have any information to corroborate that from the misdemeanour courts. However, I believe that measures were taken. I don't know how effective they were, but I believe that they did have some impact. However, not as much as was expected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you exactly mean by bringing in people? Were they detained? Were they kept? Were they taken from their houses? It's ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that -- actually, we have two categories of people that we're talking about. The first category were those who were already members of the Territorial Defence, and they deserted. They moved to Serbia and never came back during the war. Some of those who deserted from the units came back home and from their homes they would be taken back to the unit from which they had deserted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that would be for everyone who had fled? Would that be true for Serbs? Would that be true for Croats? Would that be true for Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In the course of 1991, almost all Muslims deserted. They left, although they were members of the regular JNA units. They refused to take part in TRO units, and that's why they were never assigned to any of them. So this applied only to Serbs. As I've already told you, there were only a couple of dozen Croats, and they were not important from the point of view of military obligations. And as far as I can remember, there were no able-bodied Croats at the time. None of them fell under the military obligation category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So where you say that is about people that deserted, this, although it don't say explicitly so, this order and what you testified is just about Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I presume that the document we looked at previously, the 20 April order, will receive exhibit number 834; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are all assisting Madam Registrar to find the right numbers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And can 834 be placed before the witness. He has it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, do you have in front of you the document dated 20 April 1992, an order of the Sokolac municipality Crisis Staff to the officials of the Sokolac public security station?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the date that I have on the document is 21st of April, and in the first paragraph of this order a reference is made to precisely the thing that you have mentioned, but the date is different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I see that the date on the English translation does not correspond -- or does it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that the B/C/S gives 21st of April where the English translation gives 20th of April. Could you please refer to the number. That's 0102311, 21st of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the confusion may arise from the fact that in the original, or the copy of the original, it appears the order was dated 21 April in response following the session of the Crisis Staff on 20 April, but we are looking at the same document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that an order to the public security station to undertake steps in connection with the theft of military equipment from Faletici, and in item IV, to immediately submit a report on its execution of the instructions back to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder why we keep asking the witness these things. The witness is, in effect, being just asked to confirm that he can read, with respect, because if he's just confirming every time the exact words that are in the documents, then we're not really making progress with any questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I take this to be an incentive by Mr. Stewart to speed up and see whether, by reading, we can achieve the same result as by asking it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I could ask for a simpler confirmation, Your Honour, but I'm still mindful of the encouragement long ago to make the public aware of precisely what we're talking about and trying to balance those considerations. If I've overstepped, I will go through the documents more expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's see whether we can find the right balance. And Mr. Stewart will not oppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, is that simply an order to the public security station to undertake certain steps and then submit a report back to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, earlier, Mr. Tupajic, we looked at reports to the republic level and interaction with the republic level. Who were the individuals in your municipality who maintained closest and most regular contact with the republican leadership of the SDS or Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: It was certainly the man who had most contacts with the SDS leadership and the leadership of Republika Srpska. He was Milovan Bjelovac, and then Mr. Marko Simic who was a deputy and the first president of the municipality of Sokolac. Members of the Crisis Staff had occasional contacts, but mostly with the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We contacted them when we had to resolve the issues that I have already spoken about and also a number of other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- may I make the familiar request - it's the first time with this witness - to know first of all whether he understands English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you speak or understand English, Mr. Tupajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't either speak or understand English. I only know a few words that I learnt while I still worked at the ball bearings factory of Sokolac and what I picked up from movies, that is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether you're going to use any movie language or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: They sometimes use mine, Your Honour. But Your Honour, may I invite the witness just briefly to -- or would Your Honour invite him to take off his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to take your headphones off, Mr. Tupajic. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was in relation to the question Mr. Tieger asked that's just disappearing off the screen at the top, line 8. Earlier we looked at reports at the republic level, interaction with the republic level. Who were the individuals in your municipality who maintained closest and most regular contact with the republican leadership, and so on. Now, Your Honour, there are lots of ways of asking a leading question, but that is one of them. First of all, the introduction to the question is unnecessary and not appropriate, and then the question itself contains, of course, a heavily in-built assumption that somebody was having close and regular contact, which is a very different thing from the reports that are mentioned in the introductory comments to the question. So we do suggest that in this area, and everybody knows that this is a key area in relation to this witness, nobody can fail to realise that, that it is extremely important that these in-built assumptions do not form part of the important questions. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I think splitting up that question, especially where you left it open, republican leadership of SDS or Republika Srpska, gives a lot of vagueness in the question which could be addressed perhaps in a more precise way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll keep asking questions about this area, Your Honour. I don't think there will be too many questions about it and I'll certainly make every effort to make them in a way that doesn't provoke --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart invites you to make them less leading in this respect and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- there's some merit in --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the fact that I don't respond to Mr. Stewart's comment I hope is not taken as agreement with his assessment of that, but I think it's more efficient just to move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. We all now have 25 minutes to think that over. We will adjourn until five minutes to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, let me focus my attention for the moment on communications within the SDS. First of all, did the Sokolac SDS receive orders and directives and guidelines from the Main Board of the SDS in 1991 and early 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Even that question is so much better, with respect, and easily presented in neutral form. Communications, and then leave it to the witness, please, to indicate what was received. As a marker, Your Honour, for all this line of questioning, that is the Defence's submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After having consulted the whole of the Bench, Mr. Tieger, you may proceed the way you put the last question, and for the ones to come as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, how were those communications sent to Sokolac? In what form; in writing, orally, both, or any other means of communicating?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: All the important decisions of the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party that needed to be implemented on the ground, that is in the municipality of Sokolac and other municipalities, were sent to the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party. Most of these decisions were written, but it was not the case infrequently that the president of the Municipal Board informed us orally of the decisions of the activities that needed to be carried out in our locality. Besides, the president of the Municipal Board had contacts with the republican level of the party between sessions, and we would have, accordingly, briefings between sessions as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the president of the SDS Municipal Board?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: The first president officially elected was Mr. Mirko Malovic, who later, in the beginning of 1992, left the former Yugoslavia and went to the United States. Mr. Bjelica, who had been his deputy, took over and continued to be president of the Municipal Board until two years ago when he was let go, replaced from that post by a decision of the high commission, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next exhibit, please. That's an intercept dated 27 December 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P835, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Radovan Karadzic: Well, I'm fine, what have you been doing? Bjelica: Well, nothing. Karadzic: Tell me -- well they've started -- as we unexpectedly procured quite a large amount of oil for our claimants here, we have one variant with two cisterns at Joja's. Thus do you have -- where could you -- do you need them? Bjelica: Well, we do. We don't have oil. Jugopetrol will give us petrol tomorrow, according to your recommendation, petrol from Jugopetrol, but we don't have oil. Radovan Karadzic: Through whom does it go? Through Krajisnik? Bjelica: No, not through Krajisnik. As you instructed us, the price plus three dinars for the party, of course. Radovan Karadzic: I see. Good. Bjelica: The invoice goes through Krajisnik. Radovan Karadzic: Good. Bjelica: And we registered this as public enterprise Romanija-petrol and Pale will probably do the same now. Radovan Karadzic: Good. But two cisterns of oil are on the road and Joja will receive them and he can forward them where needed. And what is the price in general? Bjelica: Well, I don't know. Some men purchased it at about 45 dinars here, at Romanija. Radovan Karadzic: Well, no, this is more expensive. It can't -- where did you get it at that price? There is no way you can procure it for that much. Bjelica: Well, at Jugopetrol, I guess. Radovan Karadzic: Oh, I see, but men cannot purchase -- this is more expensive. This comes from Kotor. Bjelica: How much is it, Doctor? Radovan Karadzic: This is -- this can be deposited to the account. They asked 58. Then I asked if they can reduce it to 56, and they wanted to give three dinars to the party. That is why you should contact Joja. Can you find Joja? Bjelica: Well, I am going to look for him right now. Radovan Karadzic: So you can arrange this with him, see to it that they find the customer. These two. Bjelica: Only we don't have the money today. This took us by surprise. Radovan Karadzic: Well, someone else can pay. Take care of that. You must always have money, because of these things -- let companies pay and then you will pay them back or something like that. Bjelica: Okay. Radovan Karadzic: Or try with a private entrepreneur, try to find a way, but it is important to preserve this channel because -- Bjelica: We must preserve it. Radovan Karadzic: Yes. It is a bit more expensive down there but we need Kotor very much. Bjelica: There are no problems down there because their company also supports itself. That is, they support someone else down there. Bjelica: Well, but it came a little late. Had it been earlier we would have provided money. Could that wait only a couple of days, until Monday? Radovan Karadzic: Well, go call Joja. Bjelica: We'll provide the money, no doubt about it. Radovan Karadzic: Good. So you can -- the contract. Bjelica: Ten, ten thirty, and also these accountants, some are away on a business trip, some are not available. We cannot manage it all at once, but we shall provide the money. Radovan Karadzic: Good, good, here. Go. This guy, what's his name -- do you know Joja's phone numbers? Bjelica: Tintor, you mean? Radovan Karadzic: Yes. Bjelica: I do, let me check it again. Radovan Karadzic: 439-777 and 439-555. That is the fax, I suppose, and his secretary will know where exactly you are and she'll contact you urgently. Contact him! Bjelica: Would you be able to come to Sokolac for awhile tomorrow? Radovan Karadzic: I'm not sure. Dzimi Mudi is coming here, and I have many other commitments. That's why I'm not sure about it. Bjelica: We are doing the work. Everything is normal. Radovan Karadzic: Excellent. I hear the municipality is functioning well now. Is this Tupajic person good? Bjelica: We are working well. Special assignments. We do that as well. Radovan Karadzic: Is Tupajic good? Bjelica: Good indeed. Radovan Karadzic: Don't -- Marko, treat him well. Don't -- Bjelica: We won't. As a matter of fact, we've talked to him this morning. It won't be any problem. Radovan Karadzic: Because it isn't -- it isn't -- it is a normal thing in a democracy that a person does not function well and when someone better comes in sight, although the first one was good, someone better comes and he gets his place and the first one goes with all honours. No more smear campaigns against individuals, et cetera, but only -- Bjelica: We did not. As God is my witness, we followed your advice without causing a commotion, without making much noise. Radovan Karadzic: -- without noise, we have to think of reputations of people and take care that they do not feel humiliated because they leave one post. Bjelica: Well, Doctor, we have one more activity for this television channel, the Belgrade channel. They sent us an offer from Belgrade, this Simovic person from the Belgrade television is coming. Radovan Karadzic: Go, get it done so that we in Sarajevo can watch it as well. Bjelica: The offer is 26.5 deutschemark -- 26.5 thousand, and we will have a meeting today with this private enterprise, with directors of some private enterprises. Radovan Karadzic: Good. Bjelica: To donate something as sponsors and we'll provide -- the party will provide some 500 thousand to 1 million dinars with the help of its men in companies. Thus our goal is to amplify the channel, that is the radio, senders of Romanija radio from 2 kw to 10 kilowatts. Even Doboj can listen to it. Radovan Karadzic: Good, excellent. Bjelica: We are going to do it now. We have already agreed to make some changes, to broadcast the second Belgrade satellite programme. Radovan Karadzic: I see. Bjelica: We'll also do it here now. Radovan Karadzic: So, and what happens then? You take that antenna and then you transmit it via -- you broadcast it, and who will be able to watch it? Bjelica: Well, they guarantee this for three or four of our municipalities here, and maybe, they say, even more. Radovan Karadzic: Good. Do not hesitate to pay more. We can pay more so we can also cover Sarajevo, or I don't know. Can that signal reach Sarajevo? Can it? Bjelica: I don't know. Radovan Karadzic: I mean, we can find an extra 20 to 30 thousand if needed, so that Sarajevo can also watch. If they have some elevation point that can also -- Sarajevo, it is worth investing some money. Bjelica: Okay, then we'll check it. I'll contact -- I'll forward this to Tupajic and we'll see. Because we won't be able to finance it alone, Doctor. Radovan Karadzic: Okay. We'll find -- we'll make Dukic pay as well, then Ostojic will pay as well. Bjelica: Okay. Radovan Karadzic: Ostojic's company will pay. Bjelica: That is why we want to go for it now. Radovan Karadzic: That Romanija should pay. Bjelica: Okay. That's settled. Then you should only need to press Ostojic a little. Radovan Karadzic: I'm going to -- well, as soon as he's back. He's not here. He wants to develop Sokolac for sure. No doubt about it. Bjelica: Well, we -- we do almost everything for him. Radovan Karadzic: He wants to develop -- he won't mind spending money on Sokolac. Bjelica: We were not in the way, no. We did everything according to the agreement. Radovan Karadzic: Of course, we need to. It is not important to us whether one firm is socially owned or private. A private enterprise that feeds one municipality is better than a socially owned enterprise that needs to be subsidised. As far as that is concerned, we do not have to do like communists. Bjelica: All in all, Doctor, we'll consider this once again, because they offered us two or three variants. Radovan Karadzic: Take the best variant. It doesn't matter if it's the most expensive one. If it can get to Sarajevo, Ilijas, and these other places, Olovo. Search the hill which can -- search the hill which is the best and let's do it. Bjelica: Okay. I'll do it right away. Radovan Karadzic: Because it is much cheaper than to do it later once again. We built roads throughout Yugoslavia using the money we had. Had we taken good foreign loans and made decent roads, the country would not have fallen apart. Bjelica: Exactly. Karadzic: To hell, the country would have not fallen apart. Okay, go look for Joja right now. Bjelica: Okay, I'm going to look for him. Radovan Karadzic: Do it. What has the priest been doing? Bjelica: Well, he's up there. He's getting involved in the matters related to education and such. Radovan Karadzic: Good. You should listen to him. He has sort of strict views but -- Bjelica: Well, I'll say, he should also -- Radovan Karadzic: Well, it should be more reasonable. He is too strict. He behaves more as if he were a Catholic priest. Bjelica: Listen, let me tell you this: Those around him in that board are also -- Radovan Karadzic: Yes, I agree that somebody must take care of morale but -- Bjelica: Generally, we do take care of it but we might -- we'll discuss this issue some other time. Radovan Karadzic: Okay, but you should invite him to all -- Bjelica: Will do. Radovan Karadzic: Invite him to all and respect him. Put him in the front row. Priests and teachers must be in the front row. Bjelica: -- all. Radovan Karadzic: Well, that's it. Bjelica: Front row. Radovan Karadzic: Okay. Then call him right now. Bjelica: Okay. Radovan Karadzic: Good-bye."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Tupajic, although I recognise that names were mentioned, did you recognise the voices of the participants in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a conversation between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Milovan Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you understand Mr. Bjelica's relationship with Dr. Karadzic to be in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Well, this conversation too confirms that they had full, direct contact, and they contacted each other on many issues. I am personally surprised that they had these contacts regarding the turnover and sale of oil. I don't think Karadzic should have gotten involved in that. That should have been left to some other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before we leave this conversation, let me just ask you about a couple of persons mentioned during the course of the conversation. First of all, the name Joja is mentioned several times. Who is that, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I think this is a reference to Jovan Tintor, who played an active part at the stage of establishment of the Serbian Democratic Party. Before the war, he had a private company, and he must have financed the establishment of the Serbian Democratic Party at least in part since it had no owned funds. He was native of Vogosca, and I believe he was a member of the Crisis Staff as well, and at some point during the war he was appointed advisor to the president of the republic, and that was Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on, there is mention of finding Dukic to pay for it, and Ostojic will also pay. Do you know who is referred to in those references?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I think it's Mr. Rajko Dukic, whom we mentioned before; and Mr. Ranko Ostojic, who in 1991, according to the programme of privatisation that was being implemented then, repurchased the state equity capital in our largest enterprise, Romanija Sokolac, which was the prime -- primary vehicle of development in our municipality. It was the most important enterprise. And at another time, he was deputy Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reference at the beginning of the conversation to Jugopetrol and the invoice going through Krajisnik, do you know what that is a reference to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know about this particular purchase they are discussing here. They mention Mr. Krajisnik. I don't know whether it was Mr. Krajisnik or his brother Mirko had an enterprise, a company together, or it was only one or the other, but it says in this conversation that invoices should be sent to companies, and this name Krajisnik is mentioned. I don't know whether it was the two brothers together or only one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the establishment of RS and the establishment of governmental authorities in 1992, were communications to the Sokolac authorities also conducted through written means and through -- and orally, as they had been during -- between the Main Board and the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I think that especially after the war began in Bosnia and Herzegovina there were few sessions of the Municipal Board. I don't know about the Main Board. And information was exchanged mainly through personal contacts of the president of the Municipal Board with Mr. Karadzic. Such communication between them --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The way the question comes across in English, the last few words, with "between," and then we've got six words, if that is the correct English interpretation, then I wouldn't have thought it was exactly what counsel had in mind as the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can clarify the question. I think the witness is directing his attention to the issue of communications but let me just clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, just to make sure that the Court fully understands your responses, you had earlier indicated the manner in which communications took place between the Main Board and the Sokolac SDS and indicated that included both written communications and oral communications. My question was with the establishment of RS political authorities, how were communications between the RS leadership and the Sokolac authorities conducted? Was it written? Was it oral? Was it both?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I think communications were combined. How many written exchanges of information there were and how many were oral I don't know because I don't have an itemised list of documents but I know both means of communication were involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were the conduits for oral information conveyed from the RS leadership to Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Oral communications came mainly through Mr. Bjelica and late Mr. Marko Simic who was deputy to the National Assembly of Republika Srpska from Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just returning quickly to the telephone conversation we just listened to, there's a reference by Dr. Karadzic to looking after or taking care of Marko. Do you know who that was a reference to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, in principle it is not pleasant to talk about people who are no longer with us, but for the sake of truth I will have to say before this Court that quite accidentally I was elected president of the municipality after late Marko Simic had to resign. The information that was available to me then indicated that some sort of embezzlement was involved and that he was forced at the time by Mirko Malovic and Milovan Bjelica to resign so that additional problems could be avoided. But not everybody in the party knew the real reasons for his resignation, and that's why Mr. Karadzic is saying that regardless of the fact that this happened, it should not be made public, he should not be rejected. But by this he reduced the credibility of the party, he damaged the credibility of the party, at least among those of us who knew about the reasons for his resignation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, can I ask you to look at the next exhibit in order. That's ET 0115-1586.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P836 [Realtime transcript read in error "P386"], Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, this exhibit is the minutes of a meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Sokolac municipality held on 15 May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Tieger, on the transcript the number of the exhibit appears as P386 where I think it should be 836 and that could cause confusion at a later stage. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to direct -- look you -- can I ask you to look at the second paragraph of the minutes following the paragraph at which the attendees of the meeting are indicated, and it's the paragraph that begins, "Before starting with the agenda..." There is a reference there to the ratification by the Municipal Board of the mandate of the members of the Crisis Staff with specific persons mentioned and further references -- further reference to the ratification later on in the paragraph, and then the next paragraph reflects the formation of a personnel commission by the Municipal Board of the SDS. Can you tell us to what extent, if any, those references reflect the power of the Municipal Board in Sokolac during that time, and in particular the president of the Municipal Board?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: All the issues pertaining to the staffing policy were in the held [as interpreted] of the Municipal Board or its narrow leadership. In the meantime, as we can see from this paragraph, there must have been a change in the composition of the Crisis Staff of Sokolac municipality since there had been a change in some of the positions and those in those positions were members of the Crisis Staff. One can see clearly that the Municipal Board gave its approval to issues at the meetings of the Crisis Staff. It also had its committee on the personnel policy that was in charge of proposing individuals who would occupy the most prominent positions in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've looked at the establishment of the Crisis Staff in Sokolac and some of the decisions it received and took. I'd like to ask you about the establishment of one other body within Sokolac, and in that connection, I'd ask you to be presented with the next exhibit, which is actually item 18 on the list, the 10 April 1992 session of the Crisis Staff, and that's 0115-1499.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P837.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, P837 is a record of the Sokolac Crisis Staff meeting held on April 10, 1992. If I could ask you to turn your attention quickly to item 6 of that meeting. There's a reference there to conducting talks with SDK and to making an analysis of directing the monetary flows to the Sokolac SDK. Can you tell us what that's a reference to and what steps if any were taken in connection with the establishment of a Serbian SDK in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I don't have that document so I can't tell you exactly what happened. I believe that the National Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at one of its meetings adopted such a decision, a decision to take out the monetary flows in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was decided in that sense that the SDK branch that had existed in Sokolac even before the war and that was closest to Pale and best equipped and had the best human resources would be the main branch of the SDK. At the Crisis Staff we discussed that in order to see how we would honour this decision. From that discussion arose tasks for the president of the board, Mr. Samardzija and the gentleman who was deputy director of the SDK branch in Sokolac. The two of them were to talk to the director, to look at the documentation, and to see where the decisions were being implemented and whether the finances that had been previously paid into the Bosnia and Herzegovina SDK were now being paid into the branch of the SDK in Sokolac into the accounts of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to money raised by municipalities through taxes or otherwise, what percentage if any went to the republic and what percentage stayed in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this was 70 per cent of all the tax money that went to the Ministry of Finances, or to the government, and the remaining 30 per cent were allocated to the municipality. There was also contribution for the health insurance and for the pension insurance, and I believe that that same ratio that was established at the time is still in force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was done through the SDK?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, although the SDK, as far as I'm familiar with the area, played a dual role. It was in charge of the financial flows but also it had the control of the payment of taxes. At the same time, the financial flows went through the commercial banks as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, let me turn my attention to another subject now and ask you this: Based on your position within the SDS, your contacts with SDS officials and any other factors you may care to tell us about, can you tell the Court who the most powerful persons first in the SDS were and then in the RS, once it was formed, in order of the most powerful and descending.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I believe that I will share with you the information that all the citizens not only in Serbian Republic but of entire Bosnia-Herzegovina had at the time. According to the hierarchy, it was Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, and the two of them had the most influence and authority which singled them out. After them there was a significant gap and then some other people who were more or less respected on account of their titles, and here I'm referring to Mr. -- late Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic, who were university professors at the time. Maybe Mr. Buha as well, and that would be that. In the regions there were some influential people. I don't know how big their influence was. I can't be a judge of that. If we're talking about the level of the Serbian Republic and the leadership of the SDS at the level of the Serbian Republic, I believe that the case was as I have just described it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So it was the same as you described for both the SDS and Republika Srpska in 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic was elected as the President of Republika Srpska, and Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik as the president of the National Assembly. The positions themselves reinforced their positions in the party and enabled them to gain the authority that was necessary at the time. Mr. Krajisnik was a member of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you meet with Dr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik during 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were such meetings. Not many of them. I remember several working meetings with Mr. Krajisnik during which I was present. There were some more official meetings, there were also some chance encounters when they came to the municipality. Since Sokolac is on the road from Pale and Zvornik and further on to Banja Luka and also on the road from Pale to Belgrade, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik and other officials of Republika Srpska passed the -- this way quite often. So I must have had a number of such meetings which were rather informal. And the only ones I remember are a few working meetings with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I turn your attention to the next exhibit in order, which is number 19 on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It would be Exhibit P838, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
